title: POW01: The Achievement Trap: Why High-nAch Breaks Leadership
author: Richard Claydon
summary: Claydon argues that the achievement drive that makes people successful individually is the wrong fuel for leadership. Opening with Maya rewriting her team's slides at 1 a.m., he draws on McClelland's later finding that the best organisational leaders score higher on socialized need for power than on need for achievement. He names the failure modes of high achievers: control reflex, perfectionist anxiety, recognition hunger, short-cycle bias and delegation intolerance. His heuristic pairs emotion with motive, so anxiety signals achievement, fear of exclusion signals affiliation, and ambivalence signals socialized power. Maya's replay shows the alternative: publish the decision, clarify roles, open information and time-box dissent. He answers objections about standards, readiness and speed, and ends with a short exercise and an ambivalence line for the next meeting.
points: Leadership shifts the metric from how much you deliver to how much gets done because of you.
High need for achievement shows up as bottleneck behaviours: control, perfectionism, recognition hunger and refusal to delegate.
Reading your first emotion (anxiety, fear of exclusion, ambivalence) offers a quick clue to the motive driving your next move.
Socialized power structures the work through framing, convening, clear roles, open information and time-boxed dissent.
Rescue is faster only once; the hidden cost is dependence, lower initiative and leader burnout.
quotes: Next day, the meeting stutters. Her leads are tentative—unsure which of their choices still stand. Decisions drift. A week of momentum stalls. Maya did great work. She did terrible leadership.
Leadership exchanges “I deliver” for “I multiply.” The metric isn’t how much you get done; it’s how much gets done because of you.

As McClelland looked inside organisations, the pattern flipped. The worst leaders over-indexed on nAch; the best leaders scored higher on need for power (nPow)—specifically the socialized form, where influence is used for collective outcomes rather than personal dominance.
Notice the emotional signature here: anxiety. Under pressure, nAch whispers, “It has to be perfect.” The hand reaches for the keyboard; the clock slips past midnight; the team wakes up smaller.
Ambivalence isn’t indecision. It’s capacity: the ability to hold competing goods (speed and fairness, clarity and voice) long enough to make a wise move, not a tidy move.
Now Maya still cares about quality. She just stops hoarding it. The team shows up bigger because her power is used to structure the work, not to do the work.
But this is faster.” Once. The hidden cost is cumulative: learned dependence, lower initiative, and your own burnout. Ask: What would make it faster next time without me?
